subsubtopic: STUDY'S DISCLOSURE OF ECONOMIC BENEFITS FLOWING FROM LAW TO CURB ACID RAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United States' economy would get a multi-billion dollar stimulus if Congress passed a law to curb acid rain, says Management Information Services, a research company in the U.S. The annual net gain to the U.S. economy would range from $7.5 billion to $13 billion. The economy would gain even though such industries as coal mining would probably lose jobs and sales.
The boost would come from spending to clean up emissions from coal-fired industrial and utility boilers. Most utilities that would be affected by acid rain controls are in the Midwest. But the study states that this region would also benefit because it has the basic heavy industry to make much of the expensive emissions cleaning equipment. Across the United States there would be a net gain of 100,000 to 194,000 jobs, depending on the shape of the final legislation.
The acid rain issue in pure dollars and cents may be the language President Reagan and those in Congress opposed to a control program understand. Will the Canadian Government make good use of this information?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to urge Parks Canada to confirm the amount of money it will contribute to the development of Grassy Island National Park at Canso. I would also like to know when this money will be flowing.
Grassy Island is the site of North America's first fishing fort. It is situated off Canso, Guysborough County.
In addition to recognizing the historical importance of this site, the development will greatly contribute to economic development in the area. Grassy Island National Park will be a tourist attraction drawing thousands of people into this area. It
will greatly enhance attempts to diversify the economic base of the area.
In response to directions from Parks Canada to obtain local funding, I have worked with community groups, the MLA for Guysborough, Dr. Chuck MacNeil, and the Mayor of Canso, Raymond White, to do just that. In this respect we are close to reaching our objective.
I now want Parks Canada to outline the details of its commitment which is to supplement the local contribution and to effect full development of Grassy Island National Park.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS TO DEBATE BILL C-18
EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS TO DEBATE BILL C-18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House we witnessed a blatant abuse of parliamentary procedure and tradition when the Government called to extend the hours of debate into the evening and until 3 a.m. in an effort to close off debate on Bill C-18. It knew full well that many members of the Opposition were fulfilling their duties and responsibilities on standing committees or legislative committees, and could not be in the House to oppose this closure tactic when it was introduced by the Government late in the afternoon.
This thoughtless, naive, bullying tactic by the Government flies in the face of our parliamentary reforms. It demonstrates a lack of respect for and appreciation of the role and responsibility of opposition Members, and it shows a disregard and contempt for Parliament, its history, and its traditions.
The Government's thoughtless and crass manipulation of parliamentary procedure encourages divisiveness between Members. This does nothing to encourage or enhance the level of civility in Parliament.
I ask the Government House Leader (Mr. Mazankowski) to intervene immediately to enact changes to the Standing Orders so that this blatant abuse of Parliament does not occur in the future. After all, the Government through its actions and attitudes ultimately sets the tone and mood of the House.

February 4, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Members will join me in paying tribute to Canadian filmmaker, Norman McLaren, who died last week at the age of 72. His 45-year career, mostly in the service of the National Film Board, produced over 60 films which stand as international landmarks of our culture. McLaren explored the frontiers of filmmaking. He pioneered a wide range of production techniques, including pixillation, which joins disparate images to create continuous action, and is now in wide use.

Norman McLaren also led the way by developing a technique for direct recording on the sound track. Throughout the world Norman McLaren was awarded more than 200 prizes for his films, including Cannes' Palme d'or, yet he did not seek recognition as a film producer.

When informed that Neighbors, his hauntingly simple allegory for the nuclear age had won an Oscar he replied, "But who is Oscar?"
For all but two years of his prolific career as a filmmaker, Norman McLaren was a civil servant. As we reflect on his passing and celebrate his work, we have reason to be proud of our National Film Board.

subsubtopic: IDENTICAL SERVICES REQUIRED FOR ALL CITIZENS
speechtext:
Last
Saturday, Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to attend a Rural Dignity meeting in Agassiz in British Columbia's Fraser Valley East riding. Six hundred people were at the meeting, and their message was loud and clear: We do not want to be consulted only to be told that you are going to close our post offices. What do we want? To be first class citizens. All Canadians want to keep their post offices.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) was present at the Monday meeting. He asked the question to the Minister and assured us we would be consulted. Consultation is not what people want. Again today we read in the newspapers that the Minister responsible for Canada Post is repeating his promise to consult people before closing post offices. Mr. Speaker, this is ridiculous, an insult to all Canadians. Rural residents will no longer accept to be treated as second class citizens. They want the same postal services throughout Canada.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS AT MONCTON SHOPS-CALL FOR EFFORT TO ATTRACT NEW INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday CN Rail announced that a further 449 jobs will disappear from the Moncton main shops by year end, 279 of which will be completely lost to the local economy.
The Government must give this matter its immediate attention. I urge that a co-ordinated effort by all government Departments be undertaken to identify and attract new industry to Moncton which will help to offset the CN decision. In addition, CN management must identify these lay-offs as technological, organizational or operational change, not work related, and have appropriate benefits applied.
I would urge that those CN unions that refuse to ratify the special agreement between Canadian General Electric and CN to employ some 578 persons at the Moncton shops, reconsider the decision and its effect on their fellow workers in Moncton. All levels of government, CN, and the unions must live up to their respective responsibilities in an effort to lessen the effects on the Moncton economy.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF RESUMPTION OF UNITED STATES' NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the United States exploded its first nuclear test of 1987. In so doing it set back the chance of a comprehensive test ban for at least five years.
The Soviet Union has given notice that its moratorium on testing would end if the United States conducted another test. The Americans have given it every reason to resume testing. They show no interest in serious immediate negotiations to ban nuclear tests.
The Americans used to argue that a comprehensive test ban could not be concluded because it could not be verified. However, when the Soviets became willing to discuss verification, the U.S. shifted ground. It argued that testing was necessary to maintain confidence in its nuclear deterrent.
However, there is another reason. American nuclear tests are also part of the Strategic Defence Initiative. Star wars already threatens the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, and American deployments are eroding SALT II. President Reagan's reliance on such unilateral action shows that we will have to wait for a change of U.S. administration before any progress can be made toward a comprehensive test ban.

February 4, 1987

subsubtopic: END OF DISPUTE AT PORT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to announce to the House today that an agreement in principle was accepted by the International Longshoremen's Association this morning at 7.10 a.m., which would end the labour dispute at the Port of Quebec City.
The union executive will present this memorandum of agreement to its members on Friday, in the hope that it will be accepted and that work at the Port of Quebec will be able to start as soon as possible, perhaps this Sunday.
I would also like to take this opportunity to congratulate all those who took part in the negotiations, and who dedicated their time and effort to settling this dispute so that the federal Government would not have to pass back-to-work legislation.
Union representatives and management have taken very seriously the advice of various intervenors in the industry who warned the two parties about the precarious situation in which the Port of Quebec finds itself today, and as a result, the parties negotiated in good faith in order to reach an agreement that would be satisfactory to both sides.
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the agreement concluded today will be ratified this Friday, which will be very good news for the people of Quebec.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF NEW POLICY-CRITICISM OF DELAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a crying shame that the Government has failed to produce its long awaited refugee policy. Former Ministers of Immigration have promised for two years that the Parliament of Canada would have a new and revamped refugee policy. The last Throne Speech promised that it would be a priority and a commitment of the Government. The current Minister said that last fall was the date. Then he changed his mind and it was to be the end of 1986. Then it was to be the beginning of 1987, and we still have no revamped refugee policy.
Rabbi Gunther Plaut did a landmark report on the current status of refugees in Canada. An immigration committee has studied the matter patiently and has produced a number of reports on the subject. Communities, churches, and various coalitions across the country have mobilized. They are now saying that they are frustrated at the lack of action on the part of the Government in terms of refugee policy.
It is time that we stop promises and rhetoric. The evidence is in. There is a new phenomenon in respect of refugees. We are
no longer going abroad to recruit a quota of candidates from refugee camps. People arrive at our shores claiming refugee status. We need a policy which comprehends the new reality and is fair to refugees. Let us have this policy so that all Canadians can be proud of our record in years gone by.

subtopic: EXTENDED SITTING-CONDUCT OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS
EXTENDED SITTING-CONDUCT OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY MEMBERS

Last night and early this morning we saw one of the most disgraceful performances which ever took place in this hallowed Chamber. They became concerned when they heard that the Coast Guard did not like this alternative. They were especially concerned to learn that a foreign company was working to satisfy the Coast Guard.

subsubtopic: INCREASED DISABILITY BENEFITS-REDUCTIONS MADE BY GOVERNMENT OF ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last June 26 this House unanimously passed major improvements to the Canada Pension Plan. CPP disability benefits were increased by at least $136 per month beginning in January, 1987.
I rise today to report the theft by the Ontario Government of these disability benefits from the people who all Parties agreed were the neediest in society. When the new increased disability cheques were sent out in January, the Ontario Government, apparently alone among all provinces in Canada, reduced the provincial payments to the disabled by a corresponding amount. Not only does this mean that the disabled in Ontario do not benefit from the disability pension increase, but the richest province in Canada used the money we provided for the poor to reduce its deficit. People could be even worse off because reductions in provincial payment levels could eliminate their provincial drug cards.
The Ontario Liberal Government is a minority Government. This unjustified and miserly action must be reversed. Members of all Parties should contact their provincial counterparts to reverse this heartless action.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and relates to his fish deal with France. Yesterday he waved the treaty around. Let me say to him that he is once again playing fast and loose with the facts. Surely there can be nothing more pathetic, Mr. Speaker, than a Prime Minister trying to justify his own actions by attempting to rewrite history.
The facts are these. In 1972 Canada had a recognized 12-mile limit. This treaty by Article 3 would have had the French out of the Gulf under that 12-mile limit by May 15, 1986; last year. In 1977, Don Jamieson, a great Newfoundlander, as the Minister of Transport will agree, negotiated a 200-mile limit. In 1980 Romeo LeBlanc negotiated the French out of that limit by May 15, 1986. What has happened is absolutely the responsibility of this Government.
Hear, hear!
Why did the Prime Minister undo the great work of the late Don Jamieson on behalf of Canada and on behalf of Newfoundland?

Mr. Speaker, the treaty has been tabled. It speaks for itself. There is no doubt as to what the treaty contains. It is very clear that in the absence of an interim arrangement there was a reversion to the provisions therein-
Where is the 1980 agreement?
-which provided, under the Liberals, for unquantified, perpetual rights to the French-
Not so.

-to fish in Canada's zone. What we are in the process of doing, with the leadership of the distinguished Minister of Transport who is the representative of Newfoundland and Labrador in the federal Cabinet-
He was.
He is in his last term.

-is a process that will protect the historic fishing rights of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador. We are most of all concerned about the rights of Newfoundlanders before anything else. We have recognized the complexity of this problem, but we know the rights of Newfoundlanders are central to any solution to it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is right that the treaty speaks for itself, but he misinterpreted that treaty today. Article 3 makes it quite clear that the French were to be out of the Gulf by May 15, 1986.

February 4, 1987
Hear, hear!
Why did the Prime Minister's officials from his office and the officials from the Department of External Affairs overrule the Canadian negotiators and make a quick sell-out to the French?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in regard to both the preamble and the essence of the question, my right hon. friend knows full well that the information on which he bases his question is completely erroneous. I am being very polite. It is an absolute falsehood.

The fact of the matter is that when confronted with a dilemma we were faced with the sellout of the Liberal Party, the Government of which he was a member, and I will allow the Canadian people to make up their minds about the true import of a treaty which had grave consequences for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador and Canada. Will the Prime Minister tell the Americans that Anne of Green Gables is not a threat to American culture? Will he tell them that even if we beam The Beachcombers reruns to them non-stop that American culture will not be at risk? In short, will he undertake to explain the facts of cultural life to the Americans, that with their population ten times ours the economy of scale is ten times in their favour and the risk is tenfold against us?
Mr. Speaker, I assume the Hon. Member is referring to a comment by Mr. Yeutter. In my judgment, his comments betray a stunning ignorance of Canada.
Hear, hear!
His remarks are completely insensitive and totally unacceptable to the Government and the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister help put an end to the ignorance of the Americans about what is meant by cultural sovereignty, specifically by naming the cultural industries not on the negotiating table, which are broadcasting, film, music, and publishing? Will he unequivocally state that those industries are not up for grabs?

Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend will take the opportunity to consult
a speech that I made in this regard at the University of Chicago, she will see it indicated among other things that:
If we and our American partners cannot strike a deal that will achieve these goals, a deal will not be struck. Our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to fight regional disparities, our unique cultural identity, our special linguistic character-these are the essence of Canada.
They are not at issue in these negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. To coin the old expression: "We are looking for action, not words". Will the Prime Minister take action against what he has properly stated as the unacceptable statements by Mr. Yeutter? Is he prepared to send a diplomatic note to the President of the United States protesting the statement by Mr. Yeutter and clearly state, so there is no mistake whatsoever in the administration, that our cultural industries and identity are not negotiable? Will he take that specific action today so that there will be no misapprehension on the American side?

Mr. Speaker, I have conveyed that view repeatedly to President Reagan, to the public of the United States, to the administration and, most recently, to Vice-President Bush and Secretary Baker. If Mr. Yeutter or anyone else would care to entertain their own view, I suppose it is a free country. However, our position is very much the one I have stated, from which there has been no change at all. If the Hon. Member wants my view of Mr. Yeutter's comments, I have already given it.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister understands full well that Clayton Yeutter is not a private citizen expressing his own view but a senior trade spokesperson for the United States Government. I believe that it requires action on the part of the Government to react clearly and officially to the declaration made by Mr. Yeutter and say that it is unacceptable. It should clearly state all the specific items that we will not negotiate and not put at risk.

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what I just said. That is my position and the position of the Government of Canada. It is very clear and has been consistent throughout the piece. Let me quote from an article on December 1, 1986, dealing with this issue and involving my hon. friend. It states:
"We want to trade around the world with every nation of the world. We don't want to lock ourselves in (with the United States)", yelled Axworthy from one microphone.
Screamed Johnston from another: "If you want to protect cultural industries, you do so through bilateral agreements with the United States".
That is the position of the Liberal Party. Our position is that they are not up for grabs.

CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE Mr. Cyril Keeper (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
That the first report of the Standing Committee on government operations, presented to the House on Monday, December 5, 1986, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to deal with this motion because I believe the Post Office plan should go back to committee. The report card on this plan given to the Minister responsible for the Post Office has an F on it.
F plus.

F minus. The Post Office plan is a failure, both in its process and its politics. The plan must go back to committee so we can hear witnesses other than the President of the Post Office. The committee must be able to travel and hear the views of ordinary Canadians concerning this plan.
Motions
I want to deal with three aspects of the plan. I want to deal with the service implications, the poor service the plan implies.
I want to deal with high postal rates. I also want to deal with the undemocratic way in which this plan was developed.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a good plan, in fact it is a failure. It is not good for Canadians. This plan should be returned to committee and the average Canadian consulted. The committee should receive testimony from the public as well as from the Post Office.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on post office services as far as the plan is concerned and on the plan's development strategy.

People are fed up with the lousy service they get from the Post Office. It has been deteriorating for probably 10 or 20 years under both Liberal and Conservative Governments, and it has to be turned around. People in rural areas feel threatened by the Post Office plan. Their fears are not assuaged by the reassurances that the Minister gives regarding rural post offices. He knows people are worried about the possibility of their post office being closed, but what does he say? He does not stand up and forthrightly say there will be no post office closures and we will improve post office service. What he says is there will be no post office closures in rural areas without consultation. We will hear what you have to say for 90 days. That does not reassure people because their experience with the Post Office has been that it is like talking to a deaf person, or a brick wall; you cannot get information out or opinion in. People have no confidence in a process of consultation involving the Post Office. When they hear the Minister give them assurances of consultation before their post offices close, what they hear is that their post office is going to be closed, because that has been their experience.
The Government plans to close rural post offices. The privatization of rural post offices is referred to as the turnover from the public to the private sector. This will involve a reduction of service. The Government talks of the amalgamation of post offices which will result in the closure of post offices. In fact, the President of the Post Office admitted in the Government Operations Committee that hundreds of post offices will be closed. He would not say when or where. People will not be told until it has already been decided that their post office is to be closed. They will have 90 days to complain about it.
Rather than taking that approach, the Government should consult with people on the over-all policy of the Post Office. The Government should ask people whether they want the national deficit reduced through cut-backs in postal service or whether they want a good postal service.
The supermailbox is the Conservative answer to door-to-door service in suburban communities. It is unjust that some

February 4, 1987
Motions
people must use supermailboxes while their neighbours get door-to-door delivery. It is a bull-headed policy which the Government cannot maintain over the long term. It is also politically stupid and insensitive. It is astounding that a Government, which is in third place in some public opinion polls, would alienate its base of support, the people in middle income suburban communities who have paid $150,000 or $200,000 for their homes. Those people pay the same taxes as everyone else but receive less service. In addition to being unjust, that is politically stupid.
After bull-headedly deciding to go ahead with the super mailboxes the Government mounted a $1 million advertising campaign. However, the boxes did not work. The $1 million spent on advertising was a complete waste. It was shown on the national news that one key would open many compartments. That is the image which was created for the boxes. Every dollar spent trying to create a positive image was completely wasted. The Government tried to foist these boxes on rural communities as well.
Mail service began to deteriorate under the past Liberal Government and has gone steadily down hill under the present Government. The most aggravating aspect is the slow delivery. I have mailed notices of meetings in my riding to businessmen and community people, as have my colleagues. These notices were mailed a couple of weeks in advance, in compliance with the published standards of the Post Office, but arrived too late. Ordinary citizens have the same complaint. It can take eight days or a couple of weeks for a letter to be delivered from one side of Winnipeg to the other. Letters sent from Vancouver to Winnipeg can take two weeks to be delivered rather than three or four days.
These aggravating delays in mail delivery turn people off. The small business community has been turned off as well by the Post Office's inability to deliver on time and efficiently. People have turned to courier services for which they pay much more. Conservative ideologues like to threaten the Post Office with privatization. However, in many respects the Post Office has already been privatized because people are paying for courier service to avoid the poor service of the Post Office. As a result, the public service is losing revenue.
Poor service impacts on the people who work at the Post Office. It results in job loss, salary cuts, and being driven into poverty. Many people believe that postal workers are overpaid. I would use as an example the cleaners at the Post Office. They used to be public servants and earned around $10 per hour. Due to contracting out they are now paid only $5 per hour. For even a single person to live on that wage in Toronto is to live below the poverty line. The policy of privatizing existing public service jobs is driving people into poverty. That is an abominable policy. I wish the Government would become aware of what it is doing and consider the consequences of its own policies.
People are not willing to accept increases in postal rates
because they are getting poorer and poorer service. Until the
Post Office is turned around, no one will be willing to pay
increased postal rates. People are aggravated by rising rates when service is decreasing. Rates have risen considerably. The Post Office has, in effect, requested an annual rate of increase. It will be coming back every year for a rate increase. It will be like the Chinese water torture. The drops will fall one at a time and it will drive you out of your mind. The Post Office must improve its service before it can justify increased rates.
The cost of many postal services other than first-class stamps has increased. Small business has rejected these rate increases because they threaten their economic survival. If there is one sector that is dependent upon the Post Office it is small business, and the rate increase for small business is a much higher percentage.
Let us consider the impact of these increases on Canadian culture which only yesterday was threatened by the American representative who demanded that Canadian culture be put on the free trade bargaining table.
Do you know his name?

Mr. Yeutter. He is threatening to strip Canada of its cultural sovereignty because he wants it on the bargaining table.
The Post Office policy affects Canadian culture with respect to magazines, such as Maclean's, the Canadian counterpart to Time, as well as other cultural and intellectual magazines and periodicals published by non-profit organizations or churches. They have subsidized rates, and increased rates threaten the existence of these magazines. Ordinary Canadians, small business and Canadian cultural industries reject the rate increases.
I want to comment on the development of the Post Office policy. This policy was formulated behind closed doors with no opportunity for public input. The Committee refused to hear public witnesses, but we intend to continue to exert pressure until it hears public witnesses. The Committee and the Minister have refused to travel. It is no wonder that the policy failed in its development and its delivery of service.
The Government's basic strategy toward Post Office policy is wrong-headed. The Post Office cannot deliver mail on time with a policy that operates on the barest minimum. We need a full service Post Office so that it can compete in revenuegenerating areas and provide cross-subsidization to those aspects of the Post Office that are costly.
In conclusion, this plan must go back to committee because it is a failure. There must be public consultation through travelling committees so that ordinary Canadians can have their say.

Mr. Speaker, I have to say that this plan for our post offices is a failure. It is a bad plan, and it should be sent back to committee so the public can give its opinion. It is a failure
February 4, 1987

because it involves a reduction in services in rural areas, in the suburbs and poor mail delivery generally.
Mr. Speaker, we must take another look at our post offices. The Minister should look at the substance and the strategy and not just the rhetoric Canada Post is spouting, if he wants to give people the assurance that nothing is going to happen, at a time when post offices continue their service reduction. This plan is inadequate and should go back to committee so that the public may be heard.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my colleague. All Members of Parliament have received numerous representations about the Post Office from their constituents. I have received hundreds of phone calls and letters from people in Regina East, lodging various complaints about such things as the supermailbox and its implementation. One constituent told me that the Post Office informed him that it would place a mailbox in a certain location but ultimately installed a different box directly below the bay window of his new home. That certainly created much inconvenience for him and his family.
Throughout most of the fall we heard various questions put to the Minister in charge of the Post Office. The Minister frequently said that these very interesting representations may be valid complaints which the Committee should consider fully. That is why I was surprised to hear that the majority Conservative members on the Committee essentially shut it down and refused to allow full and open hearings. The Committee certainly did not invite Canadians to make representations and it certainly did not travel across the country.
Many of the letters I received contained suggestions which the Committee could have considered had it been allowed to travel. Perhaps it could have arrived at a consensus which would have developed a program and policy for the Post Office that would meet the needs and desires of Canadians. Yet the majority Conservative members on the Committee simply shut it down.
Will the Hon. Member explain how this occurred? Was he aware as an opposition Member on that committee that the majority Conservative members would shut it down? What were the reasons given to him for shutting down the Committee?
It is important that we remember that the House was supposed to have gone through a process of parliamentary reform in which the Committees would have greater independence and individual Members of Parliament could represent the views of their constituents rather than those of their respective parties. There was a hope that parliamentary reform would give Canadians better legislation resulting from a consensus rather than confrontation. It is obvious that when the Conservatives shut down the Committee dealing with the Post Office they kicked sand in the face of parliamentary reform. Will my colleague give us his opinion about that?
Motions

Mr. Speaker, without trying to take partisan advantage of the opportunity, let me simply say that the Committee failed to live up to its responsibility to examine the plan that was presented to us. We heard from the President of the Post Office at some four meetings, but there were no public representations. For example, the Consumers Association of Canada was not invited to speak to the Committee, nor was the Canadian Federation of Independent Business or ordinary citizens. I wanted to hear their representations because I knew the plan had been developed in private, without public input.
After the back-bench revolt by the Tory Party when the Post Office plan was first revealed to them, it is my understanding that the Conservative members of the Committee essentially helped the Minister save face by taking the plan to committee. Then they sounded off about their own complaints. But they did not bring forward any substantive recommendations that would change the direction of the plan. That is where the failure lies. In addition, the failure lies with consulting people. So the hearings were token hearings. We needed more time to continue with them. We needed to involve the public.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask my friend to report to the House on a tour he made up in my part of the country, which is northern Ontario. He came up at the invitation of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and myself and he visited some communities with us. We met with residents in both urban and rural areas. Can the Hon. Member tell us what those people said to him? What message did they ask him to bring back to the House of Commons?

Mr. Speaker, I remember these meetings in northwestern Ontario very vividly. One was in an urban area and one was in a rural area. In the rural area the community involved was small. I went with my colleagues expecting perhaps a handful of people to show up. The meeting was scheduled during the day, and if I remember correctly it was a Friday afternoon. The turn-out was tremendous. I would say there were 30 or 40 people who attended the meeting in a small rural setting. Perhaps one-third of the entire population was in attendance. They felt that the post office was part of their community. The person who ran the library was there. She pointed out that the library could not function without deliveries from the post office. Small business people dependent on the post office attended the meeting. People active in local activities relating to the area of forestry were in attendance. Their concern was with respect to the repair of their machinery and that sort of thing. They depend upon the post office.
When we were in the urban area we had an enormous turnout. I do not want Hon. Members to think that I am exaggerating when I say this, but there were hundreds of people in attendance. They were angry about the inadequate service the post office was delivering and about the threat of continued reductions in service. These people came out in force in a small

February 4, 1987
Motions
urban northwestern Ontario community to let us know in no uncertain terms that they felt that the post office provides an essential service and that it was an abomination to try to turn it into a profit-making enterprise.
Essentially, these people recognize that it is a public service for which they have to pay through their taxes, and for its maintenance. They were enraged that they were not receiving good postal service.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today on this particular motion. Perhaps I should rephrase my remarks by saying, I am never sure when speaking about the Post Office if that is any more a pleasure than speaking in defence of borrowing Bills, death or taxes. I will endeavour to respond to a few of the concerns that my friend from the New Democratic Party has raised.
I would like to begin by saying that in my capacity as the deputy chairman of the Government Operations Committee, which has been studying the Post Office corporate plan, I am sometimes struck by the great divergence of views, and in the way in which they come together in the House of Commons. I know Members opposite are well-intentioned on matters concerning postal service, and they have very good concerns. But when I hear them talk about the proceedings of these committee meetings it is almost as if we were at different meetings. It is almost as if we were not dealing with the same issue. I hope to put some light on this particular committee report that explains to Canadians many of the challenges that face the Government, and all of us, in terms of postal service and what Canada Post wants to do.
By way of background, the Government first received the Post Office corporate plan in November. In what the Opposition and the media are fond of calling the back-bench revolt, and as a revolting back-bencher-or perhaps better stated, a back-bencher who did have some concerns about the issue-I was pleased when the Minister looked at what the Post Office corporate plan proposed and said, "I think we should give parliamentarians an opportunity to review this in the light of what they know as representatives of the people of Canada".
I think if members of the Opposition would be fair-and I do not want to accuse anyone of politicizing the matter-they would admit that, given the responsibility of Members of Parliament, in reviewing postal service we speak for Canadians. The Progressive Conservative Party is the Government. It is the Party with the greatest number of rural seats, and it certainly speaks well for rural Canadians. But members of the Opposition have asked, why don't we call witnesses? In a standing committee that is a very valid concern.
We pointed out to the NDP in particular that the March-ment Committee had issued its report. The Marchment Committee was the committee appointed by the Minister to investigate Canada Post. In fact, many of the recommendations of the Marchment Committee Report found their way into the Canada Post corporate plan. I know all Members of
Parliament have read the Marchment Report, at least if they are concerned about postal service in Canada. The appendix to the Marchment Report sets out quite clearly the number of groups with whom the authors of the report met. They met with unions, users and consumer groups. In nation-wide hearings they left not one group unheard. The report was tabled just a few months before the Canada Post corporate plan was tabled.
Let us have a look at what Canada Post is proposing. We have an in-depth report based on interviews with witnesses in hearings across the country. In the spirit of parliamentary reform, and having all of this documented evidence, why must we go back and do it again? I am a rural western Canadian. I know what my constituents want. They did not want many of the things proposed by Canada Post. So what did we do about it? The committee held lengthy hearings, some of which lasted well in excess of three hours. There were a series of meetings in which we brought the technical officials of Canada Post before us. We asked them very difficult and specific questions. Members of Parliament were able to conclude from the questions and the answers that we had some concerns about what Canada Post was proposing.
I came across as what could be known as the heavy in all of this. After hearing repetitive answers from Canada Post executives I came to the conclusion in December that I did not believe we should meet much more as a committee. I say that because the issues were far too important to let stretch out any longer. My concern was that we issue a report that was thoughtful, concise and exact. We did just that. In our report we put forward a series of recommendations. I will read them for the record and for the people who are viewing this debate. Based on that, I think everyone will agree that many of these are balanced and fair recommendations.
The opposition Parties were justifiably concerned. They said that we should travel the^country and hear witnesses. I think we were faced with the problem of trying to act quickly and effectively to ensure that Canadians are protected. We had to act so as not to make it an overly-politicized exercise in rhetoric, talk and vituperative condemnation which, God knows, this place already has too much of.
So we issued our committee report. The committee report touched on a few central issues. As a western Canadian I am perhaps showing a bias in my input. The changes proposed in rural mail delivery, the changes proposed in rural post offices, and the reductions in subsidies for weekly newspapers and periodicals are the three points that most concern me. We also had some thoughts on other issues; the delivery service in new subdivisions, the technical deficiencies of the supermailboxes, and reliability of service.
We made a series of recommendations, and the Government responded to them very quickly. In so doing, the Government and Canada Post responded in a fair and balanced manner. The qualifier that I wish to add at this juncture is that I am
February 4, 1987

not pleased with what Canada Post has done in response to at least one recommendation. That is why as a Saskatchewan Member of Parliament on the government side I have been working very hard with the Minister and Canada Post to ensure that we will see compliance, and beyond, with that one recommendation. That recommendation involves rural post offices.
I will digress and run through the committee recommendations. The committee recommended that the present pattern of rural mail delivery not be changed. We came to this conclusion as rural Members of Parliament. In many areas rural route service has been decimated by Canada Post over the last three, four, five years, and it cannot withstand any further reductions.
Generally, I do not overly politicize things in the House, but I will allow myself one political observation. Members of all three Parties had the opportunity of appearing before the committee. The hours were intentionally kept long and the forum open for as many thoughtful Members of Parliament as possible to come and cross-examine Mr. Donald Lander, the Chief Executive Officer of Canada Post, and grill some of his technical officials.
Committee records will bear out that we had so many Progressive Conservative government Members that often the meetings went on very long, and questions had to be limited because of the overwhelming degree of interest in this process. There were Members from new subdivisions, and Progressive Conservative Members from the cities talked about supermailboxes, mail delivery, and general levels of service. Rural Progressive Conservatives talked about rural post offices, rural routes, and those concerns.
The lamentable lack, particularly of Liberal Party Members, and New Democratic Party Members, was indeed disgraceful. The opposition Parties represent a significant number of Canadians. All told between the two Parties they were able to muster five Members of Parliament for an exhausting grilling on something as fundamentally important as postal service. I will leave the politics aside, but I think that Canadians should know-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member said that he did not wish to politicize things. Would he acknowledge that during each of these committee meetings not only myself as a New Democrat was there-
That's a point of fact.
The Hon. Member made an accusation-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the Hon. Member is engaging in debate. He will have the opportunity to ask questions of the Member in a few minutes.

The Hon. Member is misleading the House at this point.
Motions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Member for the Battlefords- Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley).
I appreciate the feeble bleatings, I was going to say, but that may be political. It is very important that we do put on the record the type of concern that government Members had on this issue.
So much good it did.
Myself and others were at each one and you cut off the time in the end.
How come you guys backed out on the committee?

The committee made the recommendation that the present rural delivery pattern-Mr. Speaker, I must ask your indulgence. The NDP are indulging in name calling and trying to yell me down. I ask your indulgence to call for order.
Why don't you just tell the truth?
If they were honest truths and honest points.

I am attempting to make a few points. It is very difficult when the NDP are back to their old games. I cannot hear myself think amidst this NDP heckling and complaining.
Rural route service would not be interrupted. That was our recommendation. The Minister rose in the House and said that because of the effects on rural route service to many Canadians, who are already justifiably feeling like second-class citizens with postal delivery, there would be no further closures of rural route service.
As the deputy chairman, and as a rural Canadian, I feel vindicated by that. That was the first opportunity to say no to something that I did not feel was right for rural Canadians.
The second point we made was that Canada Post would not implement wholesale closure of rural post offices. We went on to say that, prior to any considered closures, Canada Post devise and provide the committee with more specific guidelies regarding the closure of rural post offices. These should reflect regional differences and needs.
Canada Post, as part of its corporate plan, tabled a mathematical formula involving proximity between communities, number of boxes affected, and that type of variable. To those of us who live in western Canada, and rural Canada, it is impossible to establish with one formula a system for post offices that will work in Newfoundland, Saskatchewan, rural British Columbia, or Ontario. The committee made that recommendation in good faith. That recommendation was made to tell Canada Post to come back to us and let us see its plans. This was the recommendation that I had the most concern about.

February 4, 1987
Motions
In his acceptance the Minister wrote to our chairman and stated:
Although there will be cases where post offices are amalgamated and alternate postal service will be offered, this will be done over a ten year period. Canada Post does not intend to implement wholesale closures of rural post offices.
He further stated:
On the subject of the possible amalgamation of some rural post offices, I am in agreement, and so is the Corporation, with the point made by the Committee that a simple amalgamation formula cannot be imposed arbitrarily and uniformly on a country as broad and as diverse as Canada.
Canada Post recognizes the need to be sensitive to local concerns that vary from community to community. During the hearings, the President of Canada Post made the commitment that there would be no amalgamations without local consultation, and that in future a 90-day notice will be given of proposed service changes to permit this process to take place.
On the face of that, the Minister has made the commitment that our committee did make a valuable contribution. I am very concerned when I hear officials from Canada Post say that they plan on retaining essentially the same formula for amalgamating and franchising rural post offices. Obviously, Canadians and committee members will not accept having it both ways. Either Canada Post should report back to the committee before it plans any further action, or it goes ahead with what it was going to do. I do not believe that is good enough.
A number of government Members have been dealing with the Minister and we plan to have the committee again hear about this specific subject of rural post offices within the next several weeks. We are very concerned with what has happened in terms of this particular recommendation.
I know that I am taking a long time on rural service, but that is the area of particular concern to me as a western Canadian government Member of Parliament.
Other recommendations were made, for example, that the subsidies for weekly newspapers not be reduced, and that religious publications not lose their second-class mailing status.
The Minister wrote to us as follows:
The subject of second-class mail privileges for newspapers, periodicals and books is part of the larger issue of cultural subsidies for which my colleague the Minister of Communications is responsible. I should point out that the Government is presently paying more than 70 per cent of the cost of sending publications through the mail.
This particular approach has not been revisited since 1969 and, accordingly, the Department of Communications with the assistance of Treasury Board and Canada Post will be consulting with the publishing industry on this issue over the next several months.
The Minister goes on to explain that he believes that the issue of second-class mailing rates for newspapers and periodicals should not be dramatically altered. I think all of us as Canadians agree with that, but there is a difficulty which I should like to bring to the attention of members of the NDP. I was about to get political. I was going to call them the friends of free enterprise, but I will not get political. We have concessionary mailing rates for periodicals which range from very large newspapers and periodicals, such as Maclean's
magazine, on down to the Meadowlake Progress, the Maidstone Mirror, and the Spiritwood Herald, newspapers which I read in my constituency.
.
*
The New York Times.

I hear an NDP Member who invests heavily in the stock-market informing me that he reads the The New York Times.
Should taxpayers be subsidizing the profits of very large, successful enterprises, or should they continue on a cultural needs basis to subsidize small weekly newspapers? I know of no Canadian who would agree with small weekly newspapers being adversely affected. If the taxpayers of Canada are paying 70 per cent of present subsidies, I would like to have another look at some of the larger publications.
We made the recommendation that religious periodicals should not lose their second-class mailing privileges. It is selfevident, obvious, and sensible. For several months Canada Post-in fact it pre-dates the corporate postal plan-has been in disagreement with several religious publications over what it calls "sufficient content". As a government Member representing people who regularly read The Lutheran magazine, The Presbyterian Record, and such periodicals, I do not find that to be an acceptable excuse on behalf of Canada Post. Many religious publishers and editors have pointed out the concern about other periodicals receiving a subsidy and their periodicals not being able to receive some kind of mailing assistance.
In this context the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) and the Minister responsible for Canada Post have made it clear that these issues will be dealt with. We have seen The Presbyterian Record regain its full mailing status. We have seen the statement by the Minister that on a case by case basis we will look at magazines and that those which are bona fide religious publications will receive mailing privileges. Unfortunately, it is not sexy, it does not sell a lot of papers, and it does not get a lot of headlines to talk about an eminent, reasonable, and sensible position.
The Opposition gets carried away with the issue and refers to girlie magazines receiving subsidies whereas religious publications do not. If that were the case it would be unacceptable. If we review what the Minister has done and what he instructed Canada Post to do, we see that the method is being dealt with reasonably.
But The Lutheran magazine does not get it.

I hear the Hon. Member. I am aware of that. In fact, I was just in Radisson the other morning, a very good community in the heart of my constituency, to meet with a number of people from the Lutheran congregation. We spoke at some length about the matter, and I gave them my personal assurance that we would be bringing this case to the attention of the Minister. I am hopeful that upon review of The
February 4, 1987

Lutheran publication there will be no doubt about whether it should receive a subsidy.
I see Mr. Speaker signalling that my time is up. I have not touched upon five or six recommendations. I also have a few thoughts on the status of Canada Post as a Crown corporation as opposed to a government Department. I have a number of comments I wanted to make dealing with general service to Canadians. Unfortunately time constrains all of us. In the helpful, hopeful, and constructive way of which I know NDP Members are capable, perhaps they will ask some good questions and I will have a chance to clarify a few of their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should not have apologized to the House for being political. That is what this House is all about. I remember the comments of Robert Thompson. I think he was a Social Credit Member from Alberta and then he became a Conservative Member for a Fraser Valley riding in British Columbia. He became so frustrated in the House that he said: "Mr. Speaker, this House is becoming a political arena".
Keep politics out of the House!

Yes. Surely that was the quote of the decade in that this House is a political arena.
I was amused when the Hon. Member for The Battlefords- Meadowlake (Mr. Gormley) described Conservative Members going to the committee one after the other and presenting their views. It sort of sounded like lemmings going to the sea, lemmings jumping into the sea. Perhaps it is a sort of beginning for the next election. Conservative Members will be as scarce as are Beothuks now in Newfoundland.
Do you have a question?

Yes. I received a letter dated January 21, 1987 from the general manager of the Post Office in Vancouver. It was addressed to me as his Member of Parliament. He indicated that in order to streamline and enhance mail collection, they would be relocating street letterboxes. He went on to indicate that to minimize any customer inconvenience, they would be posting blue notice forms on any box being relocated or removed. The notices will inform people of the location of the nearest mailbox. Any box which does not have a notice form will remain in the same location. They expect to complete the project by February 28, 1987. If a senior citizen runs down to post a letter, she will see a blue notice posted for her convenience saying "sorry, you had better go to the other box" which could be half a mile away.
When will the Conservatives stop destroying the Post Office in Canada? They are to get rid of post office boxes in the streets of an urban riding.
It is the pick-up boxes.

The letter said that they will be posting blue notices on the boxes to be relocated. They are to cut down on
Motions
the number of boxes in the streets, the red boxes, the symbol of the Post Office.
When will they stop? How far will they cut back in postal service? In this urban area they are to get rid of mailboxes, which will inconvenience people. If we think they are mad at the Post Office now, wait until they go to mail a letter and they are faced with not being able to get the box open and a blue notice telling them to go down the street a mile. It is ridiculous.
Is this Tory blue? Is this les bleusl Is this what we are to get from the Tories-blue notices on mailboxes? When will it stop? When will they stop cutting back in the Post Office and start thinking about the convenience of ordinary Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I think the intent of the question was concern. As usual, NDP Members phrase "when did you stop beating your wife" questions. Obviously I will not respond to the tenor of the question, the usual partisan rhetoric of which they are capable. However, I think the Hon. Member's concern stems from the whole question of urban service, particularly the so-called superboxes. I know that they are a concern in the newer subdivisions of Vancouver.
When the committee undertook its study, it found that as early as 1974 Canada Post began the group pick-up box concept in subdivisions. Of course that fact made opposition Members go loony because they keep calling it the "Conservative postal plan".
Canada Post is a Crown corporation. It has undertaken some service reductions. We must weigh these service reductions in the context of door-to-door service, for example, whether taxpayers of Canada will pay for a cost of some $500 million. Will urban dwellers pay $500 million to have services extended to new subdivisions? I know that is the concern.
In respect of his specific question on the relocating of red mailboxes, obviously I cannot comment upon the specific case. As a good Member of Parliament I know he would have found out exactly why it was being done. As part of the group pickup box concept in newer areas, Canada Post is ensuring that so-called superboxes will actually be closer than the old green group boxes which many people have had in their subdivisions since 1974.
Specifically referring to his question, I obviously do not know what they are doing in Vancouver, but I know the Hon. Member would make the appropriate inquiries.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday I was in Agassiz in the riding of Fraser Valley East. After having listened to the Hon. Member's speech, I am wondering whether the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) spoke to the Vice-Chairman of the Standing Committee on Government Operations. He said he would speak to government Members upon returning to Ottawa to tell them the exact message of the people of Agassiz. These 600 people in this rural area indicated to him and to all other Members who were there that the message was clear. "We do not want you to come here to tell

us how you are going to close the post offices. We want to hear that this plan is being thrown away and that the post offices in rural Canada remain".
The gentleman said that we had every chance to ask questions at the committee. I was the Member at the time questioning the Chairman or the President of the Post Office. We had only two witnesses. At that time the motion was proposed to shut off the committee. How can the Hon. Member say that we had asked all the questions? I had only started that day and I asked two questions because I had no right to ask further questions. Why did the Member last week walk away from the committee when the Member from Winnipeg asked the Chairman of the committee to reconvene so that we could ask questions again on the Post Office's plan? How can the Member say that we had all the time to ask questions? How can the Member say that he listens to people and knows the problems of rural Canada, and yet when he is in committee he does something else?

Mr. Speaker, I will answer those questions with pleasure. First, the Rural Dignity movement is a very worthy group. I applaud the organizers of Rural Dignity in doing what they have done. It is a broad-based coalition made up of many of my friends from rural municipalities, villages, rural postmasters and postmistresses. Yes, I think they are getting the message across. They are reinforcing, along with the help of the entire rural caucus of the Progressive Conservative Government, the importance of ensuring a way of life in rural Canada. No one speaks for rural Canada like our Party speaks. Because of that I can say, without giving away too much, that the Hon. Member will find that rural post offices are safe as long as our Government and our Members are looking after that concern.
With respect to the committee, Mr. Speaker, it is lamentable what the Member, who was at some of the meetings, has said. Why did he read the drivel in Canadian Press from that little reporter who came to the committee hearings and twisted and distorted the things that I did? I am a former journalist. I know that journalists have their bad days. I will not comment on the little worm from Canadian Press who for some reason believes he has to malign my actions personally.
With regard to the particular committee to which the Hon. Member is referring, we had a motion at the beginning of the meeting to revert immediately to the rural postal service when just days before we had had a steering committee meeting and, by unanimous consent, made the decision to wait for another week or two before getting on to Canada Post. Why did I walk away, Mr. Speaker? I was in another committee meeting at the time. I was called and was told that this motion was coming up. I came to the meeting and I spoke to the motion. I said the same thing I am saying here, that the motion was needless because we had already agreed to another committee date. That is what I said. I said it. I left. Again, the little
termite from Canadian Press decided, for whatever reason, perhaps having a rough day, that somehow I had done something wrong. The Hon. Member was there and he should not be believing what he is reading in the paper when he saw and heard my explanation with his own ears.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment based on the question which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) already raised, namely, Canada Post's action in removing pick-up mailboxes in Toronto. I understand Canada Post is proposing to do the same thing in Vancouver and in other major centres. The reason that Canada Post is apparently doing this-at least the explanations I have received-were twofold: First, that Canada Post wanted to improve service, and second, that pick-up boxes on street corners were no longer used the way they were in the past because most people mail letters and other mail from office buildings. That is fine if you happen to work in an office building, but if you happen to live in a residential urban community, such as mine, which has a tremendously high population of senior citizens, I fail to see how that can possibly improve the service for people who want to use that service. But the removal of pick-up boxes is causing tremendous difficulties for a lot of people. In one area of my riding, Kingston Road, which is about two or three miles long, Canada Post sent a truck right along the whole thoroughfare and removed every mailbox. While I understand that this committee did not really study or take evidence on that particular aspect of Canada Post's operation, I certainly think it is something the committee may want to take a look at. Lack of mail boxes presents great difficulties to elderly people or to people who have mobility problems, especially in winter months if they are expected to walk an additional 10 or 20 blocks to mail a letter which, very often, you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, is their only contact with their own family or the outside world. It is an extremely important question to them.

I think that is an excellent question, Mr. Speaker. I realized in the cross-examination of Canada Post's executives the very interesting changes that took place in demographics, in work and in life habits. I think the Member would agree that, yes, most mail is now mailed from downtown office buildings, which is something I did not know or did not think of. That certainly does not diminish the importance for senior citizens of having accessible facilities where they can drop a letter in the post box. I think Canada Post should be aware of that. I know that in the areas where there are supermailboxes with the mail slots they are not going any further than 200 yards from any dwelling. If Canada Post is moving red boxes and if, in fact, someone must walk a great distance as a senior citizen, I do not think that is fair. I would hope that the Hon. Member for the Beaches (Mr. Young) with the help of all Members would get to Canada Post and make it aware of that and have the situation changed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by recalling what happened a few days ago in the House when the Minister responsible for Canada Post, and I think it was last Thursday, clearly said there would be no post office closures, and all Government Members gave him a standing ovation. Outside the House a few minutes later, we heard that was not exactly what he meant.
Again this morning, Mr. Speaker, in an article in the Montreal La Presse, the Minister said, and I quote:
Canada Post still intends to close several hundred of our 1,700 small rural post offices across this country and to privatize 3,500 more, the Minister responsible for Canada Post, Mr. Michel Cote, confirmed yesterday.
I would like to repeat verbatim what the Minister said, and I quote:
That is probably what will happen- But what is important is how it will be done.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, it means they are going to close some post offices. That is clear. The Minister said so to Canadian Press, and here is the text: Canada Post is going to close post offices. But it is all in how they will do it, which means they are going to wait and consult with us first. Mr. Speaker, this is really not consultation but information. They are going to inform Canadians in rural areas that one, two or three months from now, according to Canada Post's schedule, their post offices will be closed down. Why not tell it exactly like it is instead of playing with words, which is what the Minister has been doing for a whole week?
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals share the legitimate concerns of all Canadians about the present state of the postal services in this country. By establishing the Canada Post Corporation in 1981, the Liberal Government recognized the fact that postal services in Canada were an essential public service. That is why it gave Canada Post a balanced mandate, which included improving labour management relations. Mr. Speaker, I might point out that since then we have not had a major postal strike, and that Canada Post has been given a mandate to boost productivity, improve services and reduce the deficit.
Canadians have noticed some progress in recent years. Employer-employee relations are better and, as predicted, the Canada Post operating deficit has declined sharply, from $588 million in 1981-82 to $347 million in 1984-85, and to $184 million in 1985-86. Sadly, Mr. Speaker, improvements in productivity and service quality are not as promising, and the Liberals feel that their efforts should now be directed towards that objective.
Our approach is the exact opposite of the course set by the Government in the February 1985 Budget when the Minister of Finance made it clear that the priority of Canada Post was to reduce its operating deficit. Mr. Speaker, the situation did improve to a certain extent over five years and planning was beginning to bear fruits. In its report the Marchment Commis-
Motions
sion recommended that Canada Post be given at least five more years to wipe out the deficit. But in his February Budget the Minister of Finance said: No way, you have until 1988 to get out of the red. Canada Post management turned around and said: We are taking the necessary steps to balance our books. Obviously, these measures involve closing rural post offices, while home delivery will be only to the so-called superboxes, easy to open and impossible to close! A few months ago we saw some truly incredible scenes when Canada Post was in a great hurry to introduce this new system. It was acting on the new plan before the Minister had a chance to table it in the House. The superboxes were not introduced by Canada Post on November 5. We have been talking about the boxes for about a year, and we pointed out to the Minister responsible for Canada Post that Canadians didn't want the boxes and that they were poorly designed. But the Minister kept answering: Be patient, there is a comprehensive plan for our postal system.
Mr. Speaker, over a year ago, Canada Post started closing down rural post offices. In 1985-86 alone, 114 rural post offices were closed. Mr. Speaker, this means that on November 5, the Minister responsible for Canada Post was telling us what we already knew and what the Minister never wanted to admit before tabling the plan.
I also want to talk about consultation. The Conservative Member who spoke earlier said that the Minister was generous in allowing Hon. Members to have a discussion with Canada Post and to consult on this plan, a plan which as I said before was already implemented. Not only that, Mr. Speaker. It was a last minute arrangement. The Minister had no intention of consulting the House, but when he presented the plan to his own caucus, it probably caused a minor revolt, and that is why at the last minute, as you will recall, presentation of the plan had to be delayed because the Minister had to make some concessions and refer the plan to a committee. The committee did not sit for very long and heard only two witnesses: the President of Canada Post and the President of the Board of Directors of Canada Post. The morning when the Conservative Members decided to end committee proceedings by moving a motion to prevent us from asking more questions and hearing more witnesses so as to begin drafting our report forthwith, Opposition Members were there and prepared to ask questions, but so were a number of Government Members and they too had questions to ask. We were not given any opportunity to do so. We were convened to produce the report with which you are familiar. If I may, perhaps I should refer to this report and indicate to Hon. Members and all Canadians the points of the report on which we disagree and why. First, Mr. Speaker, we reject the Canada Post recommendation-endorsed by the committee-to implement a permanent policy aimed at delivering mail in community superboxes as a substitute for direct home delivery for all new housing projects in suburban areas.
Mr. Speaker, the action plan of the Canada Post Corporation clearly states that, from now on, which means that this is

permanent and not temporary, all new residential sectors will receive their mail in superboxes.
Mr. Speaker, this decision means that we have created two classes of citizens. One class with home delivery and another with delivery to a postal box. However, Mr. Speaker, these people pay the same taxes and the same price for their stamps. Why should they not be entitled to the same service?
As for the other recommendation, we reject what Canada Post has proposed. In this case also, to meet the deficit reduction objective of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), Canada Post wants to change the postal service received in rural areas and replace individual services on rural routes by a service of community superboxes at major intersections.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I was able to attend a meeting organized by Rural Dignity, a group which is putting pressure on the Government to cancel this plan and to ensure that rural post offices will remain open. One Saturday afternoon, 600 people met in Agassiz, in the Fraser Valley-East constituency of British Columbia. There were all kinds of people. There were parish priests, mayors, city counsellors, citizens, farmers, professionals-everybody in the area attended the meeting. Their message to the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) was clear: We do not want to be consulted. We want our post offices to remain as they are. For those people, the post office is a national presence within their community. There was even someone who rose to tell us that closing down the post office does not just mean closing down the post office-the postmaster will not be the only one losing his job. Small businesses could also close down. Because by forcing rural citizens to travel to another, more distant town to have access to postal services, they might then do their shopping in that other place. This means small businesses-the stores, the shops that are in that small town are unhappy about their post office shutting down. They may even be forced to quit themselves.
That is how the shutdown of a rural post office can cause the loss not just of one or two jobs within the post office itself, but also many other jobs in the area's economy. It means there is a social economic impact and the Government must realize what Canadians want where postal service is concerned. Why are Canadians not in agreement with that proposal? Because, Mr. Speaker, the Government, the committee that looked into that, and we hope to be able tomorrow to convince it to reopen the matter within the committee, can travel across the land and actually listen to those Canadians who are faced with a situation they find unacceptable, and rightly so, Mr. Speaker.
We cannot accept either the recommendation made by Canada Post and adopted by the Committee concerning the implementation of a rural post office franchising policy. Mr. Speaker, they are now talking about amalgamation. Well, amalgamation means closing, for if you amalgamate two post offices, each in a different village, one of them will have to close. Therefore, amalgamation means closing.
If they implement the franchising policy, we are certainly not going to keep all the post offices we have now.
Mr. Speaker, I feel the Government should be transparent concerning the Canada Post Corporation and tell Canadians exactly where it stands on this issue. In fact, through franchising of a post office under the responsibility of a postmaster which may be paid $12 an hour, it is seeking ways to have someone do part of the job for $4.50. Mr. Speaker, what Canada Post is trying to do in 1987 is to use cheap labour. Is that acceptable, Mr. Speaker?
Another recommendation. We agree with the solution proposed by the Committee which recommends that the rebates on postal rates should not be reduced and that weekly and religious magazines should not lose their second class mail status. I think it is important that Canadians should be able to receive certain magazines and newspapers at home. Our culture is at stake, and we agree with the committee that asked Canada Post to maintain the privileges enjoyed by periodicals, local newspapers and magazines. It is probably not the responsibility of Canada Post to subsidize culture. It is up to the responsible department, and it would be better if we had some kind of policy as soon as possible, because if the Government wants Canada Post to balance its books, Canada Post has to take care of delivering the mail and providing postal services, not culture. So I hope we will soon be advised of the Government's policy on cultural subsidies for the delivery of these papers and journals.
Mr. Speaker, we certainly cannot support the recommendation made by Canada Post and adopted by the committee that Canada Post be authorized to publish the proposed rate increases, in the Canada Gazette: an increase of 2 cents for first class mail and 9 per cent of the average rate applied to businesses. Mr. Speaker, we have a situation where services are being cut, home delivery is being phased out, post offices are being closed, and now they want to take away second-class mail privileges for certain types of newspapers.
First class mail will cost 2 cents more and the increase for all other postal services will be almost 10 per cent. In fact, Mr. Speaker, what is happening? It will cost more for reduced services. We object to that, and should the Government go to the trouble of consulting Canadians, Mr. Speaker-not information but meaningful consultation-it will find out that Canadians are quite prepared to pay a little more for service, for home delivery, for the assurance that rural post offices will remain open and that the postal service will really be up to par.
You are indicating that my time is up. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
