Mr. Speaker, first, I wish to congratulate my colleague for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) who has done a quite remarkable job in the last few
February 4, 1987

months. He has travelled extensively and consulted many people to collect all these protests against the initiative of the Government.
I have been in politics for eight years and I do not think that any issue has provoked us many comments, letters and articles.
I receive every day at my Ottawa office very emotional messages from senior citizens and people who live in remote areas and who are very worried about the Government's initiative. Naturally, as my colleague has pointed out, the Minister has said on a few occasions that no post office will be closed. However, he very quickly corrected or modified his statement by saying that some post offices would close, but only after consultation. He also added: We shall go to the regions and consult the people because we want to know what they think. He concluded by saying: In any case, we shall give them adequate notice. In fact, this process is not really consultation, but simply an exercise in telling these people that they will lose within a very short time the essential services they now enjoy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question to my colleague who has so eloquently expressed the many concerns of Canadians. During all his travels and at all those meetings, how are the people reacting to the possibility that the existing service will be considerably reduced? In addition, as I am aware of his concern for small businesses, I would like him to explain what tragic consequences the Government initiative could have on many small businesses in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question, and I would like to answer immediately the second part of that question which concerns small businesses. This afternoon indeed-and of course until this morning we did not know this debate would take place-I had scheduled a meeting with the Canadian Federation of Independent Business to discuss that postal problem. Of course, all Hon. Members received from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business a letter in October strongly opposing any postal rate increases. We are as much aware of course as the Federation that we have a deficit problem, so we must reduce it, and this is why this afternoon we met probably to discuss and find the means to eliminate that deficit problem, not only by reducing services, but perhaps also to find means of increasing revenues without thereby increasing the burden for users of postal services.
Concerning what people say whenever there are meetings, as I said earlier, I already was in Vancouver; Monday I will be in Toronto, and I have already met groups in Montreal. In Montreal, for instance, there are at least sixteen postal urban areas. Those are people who protest, and they are people who had a chance to save their money and buy new homes. And now, because they bought new homes, they are penalized and will not be able to get home delivery as other people do who bought their homes perhaps four or five years ago. This is something of course that people do not accept. They feel they are second-class citizens. There are even people who feel court action should be taken, and they are talking about having
Motions
groups formed to take legal action under the Canadian Charter of Rights. They feel this is discrimination. Why should someone who has a home on Montreal Island, especially in the Montreal area, not far away, three or four blocks away, get home delivery? Why have it on one street and not two or three blocks away, even for new homes? I know that in Toronto and Vancouver the same problem exists.
There are, for instance, people who write or phone us saying that upon coming home after work to the beautiful houses they just bought with beautiful lawns, they find holes in which Canada Post, without notice, has started pouring concrete in order to put up the famous superboxes, which as we know, Mr. Speaker, are easily forced open. The keys are no good, or one key will open them all. Of course people are mad at the way Canada Post has wasted money on those superboxes. A contract was signed without even a guarantee on those boxes.
When one figures out that the difference between home delivery and superbox delivery is $30 per house, it is no wonder people do not accept that. Without dwelling too much on rural areas, I think I already stated how, for instance, people in Agassiz, in Fraser Valley East, are concerned about those measures.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend the post office critic for the Liberal Party. I know very well that the Liberal Party is always most progressive when in the Opposition, but what is the difference between the present Liberal policy on post office and the policy of this Government? If I remember correctly, the Liberal Party introduced the green boxes a long time ago, eleven or twelve years back, and now we have the superboxes. What difference is there? Also, if the Liberal Party were in power, what would have been the difference between the Liberal Party and this Government now?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party for that question, because it gives me an opportunity to explain the difference. Yes, there is a difference. Let us start with the urban areas. It is a fact that under the Liberal administration Canada Post or the Post Office Department put up green boxes. We never denied that. But it was a temporary measure, until let us say, that community would be organized and the postal service would be gradually provided. I can say that in my own city, and this is the argument, I already had a discussion with the Minister who said: This has been a Liberal policy since 1974. Saint-Leonard, Ville d'Anjou, in my constituency of Saint-Leon-ard-Anjou, are cities that developed over the last ten years. Still, we all have home delivery, except smaller sections which had remained undeveloped but were developed after 1984 and which get their mail through postal boxes. At that time, we could get organized. But since November, people know very well they no longer will have a chance or the possibility of getting home delivery. So, the difference is that this Tory Government authorized Canada Post mail delivery to postal

February 4, 1987
Motions
boxes as a permanent policy. So, from now on, Canadians no longer can hope that six months perhaps down the road they will have home delivery, unless the Minister in charge of Canada Post drops that corporate plan.
As far as rural areas are concerned, I think Hon. Members can check the record, because I believe under the previous Liberal administration we did not close down post offices, we opened new ones.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I would like to begin by thanking my colleague, the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), for giving us the opportunity to have this relatively short discussion in the House of Commons on a matter of interest to thousands of Canadians. I would like to thank him for his perseverance in committee, as well as in the villages, towns, and cities of Canada, in keeping the concerns of Canadians alive. He has fought against the actions of Canada Post which were precipitated by the policies of the Conservative Government of Canada.
We keep thinking that we finally have an unequivocal commitment that this will not happen. Then, lo and behold, the Minister goes out of the House and says something slightly different. He leaves the door open and seeds confusion about what will happen.
I was interested in the speech of the Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley). He indicated that in a couple of weeks the matter of whether or not rural post offices will be closed or merged will be brought before committee. I was pleased to hear that because it means that my colleague, the Member for Winnipeg North Centre, has successfully badgered the Conservative Members of that committee into coming to their senses. He has planted a seed, which is now germinating, into another hearing on this very vital issue. At the end of my comments I would like to assist Conservative Members in that continuing review.
I have spent a fair amount of my time on this issue along with my colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), and the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry). Together we represent all of northwestern Ontario. Many of our citizens rely on the mail for the vast majority of their communications. Regardless of whether they live in isolated homes along the highway or in small villages, they count on the postal service. It is essential for them. The Member for Winnipeg North Centre has been to Hurkett, Kakabeka Village, and Thunder Bay to hear the concerns of citizens, consumers, business people and unions with regard to the operations of Canada Post. It was very clear that there was no demand for cut-back in service. In fact, there was a demand for increased service because people recognize the essential nature of the service which Canada Post should provide.
Part of our job in this House is to pass along to our colleagues the thoughts and words of citizens of the country with regard to Canada Post and its services. Let me begin by quoting from a letter and resolution by the municipality of Neebing within the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan. This letter, which was sent to Mr. Lander, President of Canada Post Corporation, states:
Re: Reduction in Rural Mail Service
Enclosed please find a copy of a resolution passed by our Council regarding proposed reductions in postal service in the rural areas.
Members of Council wish to express their concern to Canada Post Corporation that the suggested changes will not only serve to isolate rural residents, but will also impose undue hardship on those individuals who will be forced to travel 25 to 30 miles (each way) to obtain their mail.
It is hoped that Canada Post will attempt to develop more practical approaches in reducing its costs of operation, that will not impair the quality mail service to rural residents.
Many citizens of my riding have written to me to express their concern about what the Government and Canada Post may or may not do with postal service, and also to indicate their support for a postal system.
I will read a few excerpts from letters without naming individuals because I do not have their permission to do so in the House of Commons. However, I know they will be pleased that I have taken the opportunity to read their concerns into the record. First:
As a rural resident and a user of the Nolalu Post Office-
A small village Post Office in the rural part of my riding:
-I am quite angry at the proposed closure.
We have been told that the reason for the closure is that the Post Office is not creating enough revenue. Since when is the Canadian postal service a moneymaking business? Is it not a service supplied to the public, paid for by the public?
Has any of the government officials involved in the decision of closing the Post Offices lived in a rural area and used them? Perhaps if they did they would understand our situation.
We, the public, have been told that we will have to use the Post Office in Kakabeka Falls. This office is 24 kilometers from here. Most families, in this area, only have one vehicle. How can we use the Post Office when the hours are not suitable. Most people work and cannot get their mail between 9 and 5. What happens when our bills come late and we are charged interest because we can't get to the post office on time? I will certainly not pay the interest when it is not my fault.
Another letter comes from a gentleman who is widely known in all of northwestern Ontario. He is an elderly gentleman who writes:
Our postal service at Nolalu is being discontinued. Because of a severe cardiac problem I am unable to come and go.
Could you and your Government see fit to continue this service to we who do not live in 'favoured' places.
These letters show varying concerns of people in rural communities. Another letter states:
I am writing to you and other members of Government who were put in office to represent our needs, that I myself and other residents of my township are not in favour of having our Post Office closed, and therefore bringing this matter (our needs) to your attention for help in saving our Post Office.
February 4, 1987

Our employees of our Post Offices have volunteered to stagger their hours of working to meet the needs of our residents to enable them to have access to the Post Office, but the Government dictates the hours for the Post Office. Therefore, the residents of the community can't use our Post Office, and therefore the Post Office is not meeting its revenue. Most of the residents of our community work Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. We are at least a good 30 miles plus out from town, so therefore many residents are leaving for work at 6.30 a.m. to 7 a.m., and not returning back home until 6 p.m. to 6.30 p.m. at night. The hours of our Post Office are Monday through Friday 8 a.m. to 2.30 p.m., and closed on Saturdays. My question is, how are we supposed to put money into our Post Office with those hours? Why can't the Post Office have the hours to meet the needs of the residents of our community?
I could on and on to talk about letters, cards and phone calls. Next to questions about unemployment insurance cheques, the largest complaint in my constituency concerns the level of service by Canada Post. People are unhappy about the delay in mail delivery. They are unhappy about the possibility of losing services.
They tell me that they do not want supermailboxes because it will not provide anything new to them in the rural area. They already receive those services and more, with mail being dropped off at the end of their driveways.
People have told me that while it may not be authorized, they can leave money in the mailbox so that the mail deliverer can put a stamp on the letter and leave change in the mailbox. A supermailbox cannot provide that service.
I want to talk about central post offices in communities where there are no rural routes. These post offices, which are within a reasonable distance for those in the community, become a focal point for activity. We hear about campaigning and canvassing at small community Post Offices which open at ten o'clock in the morning because citizens congregate there to pick up their mail and conduct community business. That activity will be destroyed if rural post offices are eliminated.
While we thought the issue had been resolved, the Minister re-opened it as a result of comments he made in the House recently. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) said, as quoted at page 2979 of Hansard on February 2:
-I can give the Hon Member the assurance that there will be no closures or service changes at the Canada Post Corporation and its rural Post Offices until the recommendations proposed by the Committee are acted upon. Mr. Speaker, the recommendation referred to a period of consultation with the Canadian people on the post offices that might be affected.
Clearly the inference is that the Government will consult and talk to local MPs and others but will make the ultimate decision. There is nothing in the Minister's response to indicate categorically that not a single rural post office will be closed. The Minister is talking about a process that is not new because before this information was revealed Canada Post had been sending letters to my constituents saying that it would stop their particular routes. That was its method of consultation, but it quickly backtracked once we became organized.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: That is rot-gut, and you know it.
The Hon. Member says: "That is rot-gut".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Table the letters.
Motions
Perhaps he would like to see the letters that were delivered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: Send one over to me.

I do not have them here but I will give the Hon. Member a copy of the information. It was very clearly a retraction by Canada Post when it realized it had been caught. Is that the Government's version of consultation? Our experience leads us on this side of the House to believe that the Government will attack post offices one at a time until they are closed down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: Stop spreading fear.

The Government will close them down one by one in its blind devotion to making the Post Office break even. I wish it had a blind devotion to making it work better because people would then have more faith in the Post Office and begin using it more often.
I invite the Hon. Member to participate in the debate. Perhaps he could tell us why mail that is destined for Thunder Bay or leaving Thunder Bay must go to Winnipeg to be sorted? The result is that some of our mail ends up in northern Manitoba and we receive mail belonging in northern Manitoba. This adds many days to our delivery service. Rather than using the plant in Thunder Bay to process mail efficiently, Canada Post is so concerned about cost recovery that it goes to obscene lengths in an attempt to squeeze every nickel and dime out of the system. It should focus on improving the service.
Why was there the development of an independent parcel delivery system in Canada? It was not because of this Government but because the previous one did not put enough emphasis on quality of service to ensure that there was no need for a private parcel service. Because that was not emphasized, one now exists. It is competing with Canada Post and taking revenues away from it.
Why did the Government intervene at Canada Post when it was experimenting with a mail order shopping service which would have allowed people in small communities to buy items through catalogue shopping, thus increasing the revenue of the Post Office? Why did the Government quash that? Was it again as a result of blind devotion to ideology as opposed to a willingness to garner enough revenue for Canada Post to provide those services? That is the real question that has to be considered.
Tomorrow, at the appropriate time, I wish to table in the House a petition signed by residents from the South Gillies, Nalalu, and the Kakabeka Falls areas, residents who are concerned about their postal service. The petition is clear. It was written by the petitioners. It was not something we provided a thousand copies of and said: "Go out and fill this and we will raise it in the House of Commons". They initiated it. They clarified the preamble and the prayer to ensure that it

February 4, 1987
Motions
conformed with the rules of the House of Commons. This petition is from an organization of concerned citizens who want to ensure that their post office is saved.
This is not a matter on which we will be silent. My colleagues and I will continue to press the issue. We recognize that the main problem is not with Canada Post. It has to abide by the mandate that the Government of the day gives it. Clearly, what we have to do is change that mandate. It is simple. The only real way to change that mandate is to turf out the Government. We must then put in place a Government which believes in service to the people and not cut-backs, not squeezing. We must put in place people who believe in efficiency with quality care and quality service.
I feel the matter needs more airing. It is important that we heed the words of the Hon. Member who spoke on behalf of the Conservative Party earlier in the debate with respect to the need to continue the dialogue. Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
the first report of the Standing Committee on Government Operations
presented to the House on Monday, December 15, 1986, be not now concurred
in but that it be recommitted to the committee for further consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I find that the Hon. Member's motion is in order. We will now proceed to the 10 minute question and comment period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member who just spoke, who played along with what appears to be current New Democratic policy, which is to frustrate the objectives of Government in getting on with the business of the House, and who joins with and is strengthened and comforted by his companions in sometimes questionable law, could respond to three or four points which I wish to make.
The NDP voted with the Liberals and ourselves to create a Crown corporation. I ask the Hon. Member to respond to the following questions. Why did they do that at that time? Why did his Party participate in that decision at that time? We were seeking self-sufficiency for the proposed Crown corporation within five years. Why has the Hon. Member now changed his mind? Why are he and the members of his Party now going down another road? Why are they now playing another tune? To what fiddler are they dancing now?
As I suggested, they advocated and supported a Crown corporation which would be self-sufficient in five years. Yet, today, they are advocating positions that would add six cents to ten cents or more to the cost of mailing a letter in Canada. Why have they gone in that direction? Can the Hon. Member answer that question? What philosophy is the Hon. Member serving? He is a socialist, and I accept that. I work with him. He is a hell of a nice fellow, but he is inconsistent.
Don't accuse him of being a Tory. That's like being a Progressive Conservative.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: Socialists like the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) are opposed to the use of the private sector in any context whatsoever.
What are you talking about?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: I sit here and listen to you day in and day out, year in and year out. I accused the Hon. Member a bit earlier of being sophistic in his argument, and he was. Sophistry is not becoming to Members of Parliament. The Hon. Member knows that. I tell you to be careful. If we throw out Mr. Lander you will have no postal service whatsoever in Canada. You foster and you breed in the rural areas of the country a mistrust and uncertainty that is not becoming the Parliament of this country. You are using unfounded arguments. You are supporting your unions. Your unions are supporting you in fostering this unrest.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have heard on approximately 10 different occasions over the course of the last few minutes the Hon. Member refer to another Hon. Member with the word "you". "You" is usually referred to when one is addressing the Speaker, as I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker. I trust Your Honour will bring my colleague across the way to order and have him address the Chair in the way that is customary in this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the Chair. Of course I have been around here long enough to be fully aware that I must address you, Mr. Speaker. In the past I have been accused of asking the Speaker whether or not he would ask an Hon. Member why he feels he can be sophistic.
I would ask the Hon. Member why it is that he and the members of his Party find it so convenient today to take a position that such a short time ago they did not take. Does the Hon. Member not want the Crown corporation to be efficient? Does he want to support the unions in trying to bring down the efforts of the Crown corporation? It is less than perfect. There will not be wholesale and massive closings of rural post offices. There will not be massive changes, as the Hon. Member argues. Indeed, I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Hon. Member whether or not he would care to send me these hundreds of letters which he is receiving and to which he referred a little while ago.

The letters have already gone to the Minister and to the President of Canada Post. The question about cost recovery over the long term in terms of breaking even will not occur overnight, or in two years. That is insanity.

I am pleased to participate and comment on the important motion put forward by my colleague for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).
February 4, 1987

I rise on behalf of my constituents in Burnaby to express serious concern and anger at the manner that Canada Post has responded to the community of Burnaby in terms of service. Canada Post is seeking increases in postage rates at the same time that it is seriously eroding the quality of service to our communities.
We were recently informed by the regional office of Canada Post in Burnaby that some 130 street letter boxes were to be eliminated. There was no consultation whatsoever with the local council. The Mayor has expressed his very strong opposition to this plan. There was no consultation with myself as the local Member of Parliament. Instead, Canada Post simply dictated to the people of Burnaby that they will lose this service of 130 street mailboxes. At a time when Canada Post is seeking an increase in postal rates, that heavy-handed attitude is absolutely unacceptable.
We have been told that a small blue sticker would be placed on the mailbox that will be eliminated, and at the end of a month that mailbox will be gone for good. This is a direct result of Conservative government policies aimed at cutting back on the quality of postal service in communities such as Burnaby.
Why was there no consultation with the people of Burnaby before this type of decision was made? Why has the Post Office insisted on cutting back service in other areas? Recently I was successful in having a sub-post office reinstated in south Burnaby at the Metrotown area. Until that time, the previous sub-post office had been entirely eliminated. The service at the south Burnaby post office was completely inadequate. It had long delays and line-ups.
Myself and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party insist that before there is any increase in postal rates, service be improved. Far from being improved, as a result of the cutbacks in mailboxes, the poor service, and the lengthy delays in delivery, there has been a deterioration and erosion in the quality of mail service in Burnaby. The Conservative Government is responsible for this decline in postal service.
I am pleased to rise today to support the motion of my colleague which calls upon the Government to come to its senses and restore quality postal service in Burnaby, and elsewhere in Canada.

It is clear from what my colleague has said, and when comparing what has happened in my riding, that it is typical Conservative thinking that the best way to get at the Post Office is to make it more difficult to use, so let us eliminate as many of the drop boxes that we can, and let us restrict the hours of operation of the post offices so that people cannot get into them. Quite clearly, I am wondering whether the Government wishes the Post Office to fail. What is its ultimate game plan? Is it trying to shut down the Post Office, or is it setting it up for privatization? What is the Government up to?
Motions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway)

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make some comments with respect to the first report of the Standing Committee on Government Operations in connection with the Post Office. I am also pleased to have the opportunity to comment on the amendment put forward by the NDP, and also to make some general comments with respect to the Canada Post situation in my constituency.
I listened with interest to the first comments made by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) from the perspective of rural Canada. I also listened with interest to the comments of the Hon. Member for Saint Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) from the perspective of a new community with growing suburbs and new homes that were without postal service. I then listened to the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and his comments dealing with the situation from the perspective of northern and rural Canada. Then I listened to the comments of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). The comments of the Hon. Member for Burnaby sounded somewhat familiar to me, because I have the perspective of an urban Member with a long established constituency. It is not a constituency with rural postal routes, or one that has new subdivisions blossoming up. It is a long established community with some modest changes, some infill, some increases in density, some new apartment buildings, and some new townhouses. There are no vast changes or vast rural areas. I see the situation a little differently, and so do my constituents.
When I was first elected to Parliament two and a half years ago I was personally aware, and I knew from the comments that had reached me from my constituents, of an uneasiness about the postal situation. That uneasiness has gone up and down over the last few years. The Post Office is not a problem that has suddenly burst upon us over the last two and a half years.
It has been apparent for some time.

It has been with us for some time, as my Liberal colleague says. In fact, it dates back to the days when the Government that he supported was around. We went through some fluctuations in mail service, particularly with postal strikes that were rather devastating to the services that we had. We seemed to come out of those strikes and into an era with irregular postal service. We did not seem to be able to put it all together. Somehow the Post Office never seemed to be able to put it all together, the way it seemed to be in what I would refer to as the good old days, the days that I recall when I was a boy growing up, and even a few years ago when the postal service was something that could be counted on. When you put a letter in the box, it would be delivered to where it was going within a day or two. Those days are long past. They did not pass within the last two years, they have been long past for some time.

February 4, 1987
Motions
The Hon. Member for Burnaby referred to the problem that I and my constituents have been having, that is, the removal of the street letter boxes. That is something that has hit my constituents very severely. It arrived in the last few months in the constituency of York East and in the surrounding constituencies. I hear from residents in various constituencies around, particularly from Broadview-Greenwood, the Beaches, and also from Don Valley East and Don Valley West. I know that the Members for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) and Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) do an excellent job in looking after those problems. But at the same time I certainly hear the rumblings when the street post boxes are removed.
I might say that dozens and dozens of these street postboxes have been removed in my constituency. Every time that one is removed, I receive telephone calls and letters. Recently I have been receiving petitions. In each case I have been in touch with Canada Post and with the Minister responsible for Canada Post, urging them to replace those street letterboxes. I do that not just because I receive one or two telephone calls and some petitions, but because of the composition of the population in my constituency, the demographics of it. The fact is that it is very substantially made up of senior citizens. My constituency has more senior citizens in it than any other constituency in Canada, with the exception of Victoria, British Columbia.
When one of these street letterboxes is removed in my constituency, it is not just a case of it disappearing and the residents being able to go a few blocks away to find another one. My constituents and I are faced with a problem. They are senior citizens. In many cases they are relatively immobile. It is just impossible for them to get to another letterbox which is in any way convenient. In fact, many of them have drawn to my attention that they actually had to take a bus or a subway train to get to a place where they could mail a letter. That is ridiculous to them and ridiculous to me. Surely it must be ridiculous to Canada Post and the Minister responsible.
Fortunately, a number of these street letterboxes have been returned at the urgings of constituents and at my urgings. These petitions have been effective in getting back some of these postboxes. I am hopeful that we will be able to get a lot more of them back in the very near future. I am certainly making representations right now to the Minister. I am optimistic, I might say, that he and the President of Canada Post will see the light of day and return these street letterboxes.
I was interested to hear the Hon. Member for Burnaby say that his constituents were receiving some notice of the fact that postboxes were being removed. That has not happened in my constituency. I am surprised to hear that it has happened in any constituency across the country. However, in the cases where they have been removed, I have been hearing about them in a hurry, as have other Members of Parliament. Once again, I am optimistic that we will have a goodly number of those street postboxes returned to us.
That particular problem struck my constituency just prior to Christmas-time, just before the next great problem with Canada Post-the question of taking away second-class mail privileges from religious publications. That is a particular difficulty in my constituency because it is the home publication base of The Presbyterian Record. Not only is it published in my constituency, but it is the location of the head office of the Presbyterian Church of Canada. In addition, the editor of The Presbyterian Record is the Minister of St. Mark's Presbyterian Church in my constituency. As one might imagine, there are many members of the Presbyterian Church of Canada who receive The Presbyterian Record on a regular basis. Suddenly they have been faced with the prospect of an extreme escalation in the price, affecting not only the church itself but those who have to pay for it, the church members. They were understandably concerned. They were in touch with me and with other Members of Parliament.
After representations by myself and other Members of Parliament, after petitions and letters which deluged Canada Post, the Chairman of the Board of Canada Post and the Minister responsible, I am pleased that the President of Canada Post announced that second-class mailing privileges were being restored to The Presbyterian Record. This proves that one can get some positive response if one makes the proper waves and rattles the bars enough. Hopefully other Members of Parliament will do that for other religious publications. I heard today that The Lutheran publication is having the same sort of problem.
That problem landed on our doorstep, as I said, just prior to Christmas-time. At about the same time another problem landed on my doorstep relating to the whole question of new subdivisions. We do not have vast new subdivisions in York East, but we have new apartment buildings and townhouses. One extremely peculiar situation came to my attention from one of my constituents relating to a townhouse-apartment building complex, a co-op housing complex, built in a triangular shape and fronting on three streets. Two of the streets are prior existing streets and one is a new street, a brand new street. The townhouses and apartment buildings built on the existing streets with existing names receive door-to-door delivery. The townhouses receive door-to-door delivery even though they are brand new. The apartment buildings built on existing streets in the same complex receive the usual apartment mail delivery in mailboxes in their lobbies. However, on the new street, which is part of the same complex, the apartment buildings receive the usual apartment type of delivery and the townhouses have green boxes, soon to be replaced by superboxes, I suppose, sitting hundreds of feet away.
It makes no sense at all. It is one housing complex, but the situation exists because of a technicality that some of the townhouses were built facing a new street whereas the other ones were built facing existing streets. The ones on existing streets receive door-to-door delivery and the others do not. It makes no sense at all.
February 4, 1987

Once again we have made representations to the President of Canada Post and to the Minister responsible. I hope, for heaven's sake, that they are listening to this debate and that they will straighten out the mess and ensure door-to-door delivery in that portion of the complex as well.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. For some time now the Hon. Member has put on record his concerns about postal service relative to his constituents. I am sure he is sincere. I wonder whether he would take this opportunity to move an extension of the hours, so that we could vote on the resolution and get the matter to committee for a full hearing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway).

Mr. Speaker, those are three concerns in connection with the Post Office which have been pointed out to me and which I have taken up on behalf of my constituents.
Another concern was raised immediately prior to Christmastime. It concerned the Christmas card system of mailing last
Motions
year. About a month and a half prior to Christmas, Canada Post suddenly introduced an incredibly silly system whereby one had to buy special envelopes in order to obtain a decent lower rate for the mailing of Christmas cards. If any other government body or private company had introduced a system with such incredibly short notice like the one utilized by Canada Post, they would have been shot.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. I want to draw to a close, but let me say that I cannot support the amendment of my colleagues in the NDP. However, I support the motion to endorse the first report of the committee because I note that it provides for a continuing review of Canada Post by the Standing Committee on Government Operations. That is exactly what we need. We need a watch-dog on Canada Post, and this committee will do the job.
